review:
I liked Tropico 3, bought Tropico 4 and LOVE it.   I didn't think Kalypso/Haemimont could screw Tropico 5 up.  They did.  The game has far less content than Tropico 4 did on release day.  This is so you can buy content later as DLC!

The economy controls are dumbed down.    Rent, wages, and all other economic factors are frustratingly simplified and broad. 

Shipping was a bit of an annoyance in Tropico 4,  goods could stack at docks faster than it could be shipped.   In Tropico 5, that has been remedied (sort of) but the new way of shipping goods is an annoying, island clogging, minutiae-filled chore that makes me long for T4's flawed but ultimately less annoying shipping system.

T4's troops worked automatically and you had no control over them.  In T5, you do have control.  A good thing, right?  Wrong.  The troops controls are clunky and unresponsive.  Another chore, not fun.

Rebels in Tropico 4 would appear if you were doing things wrong or didn't have enough jobs.   There was a reason (and cure) to having rebels on your island.  In Tropico 5,  you have rebels for no reason.  Your island could be a perfect paradise, but huge rebel attacks will still occur.  The Developers have admitted the rebels are arbitrary and for no reason other than some lame excuse about it being an upstart island with political turmoil; it just (and does, often) happens.

In Tropico 4, you could be a benevolent ruler, or a brutal Tyrant, which is what Tropico was all about.   In Tropico 5, you are an impotent and weak  governor that can only survive by doing your best in hopes of  pleasing the fickle masses to desperately stay in power.

Then there is DLC.  Tropico 4, when it came out, was quickly buried in DLC. BUT!  The first several DLC were handy, useful DLC.  The DLC had VERY useful buildings, cool decorator pieces, a mission, and outfit.   Over time though, the Tropico 4 DLC became cheap, useless cash grabs.   This crappy DLC content continued on into Tropico 5.  All the DLC in Tropico 5 is pointless and adds nothing interesting.  Not only that, but a few skilled gamers actually found large chunks and entirely complete, usuable DLC in the RELEASE DAY game files.  Which the Devs tried to patch out and B.S. away.

In Hindsight, you could offer me Tropico 5 for free, and i'd decline the offer.  Tropico 4 is superior in nearly every way.  With Tropico 4 being available on Steam, there is absolutely no point, reason, or need to buy Tropico 5.

This really, for me, is a bummer.  This isn't some game I saw, tried, and didn't like.  I LOVE Tropico 4.  I WANTED to see this game succeed.   Kalypso/Haemimont are the little guys in the gaming industry.  But when they got greedy and released a content-weak game and put that content (that isn't that great to begin with) in DLC, they sold their integrity to nickel-and-dime their customers.

I was dissapointed when  Kalypso started rushing out several shoddy DLC at the end of Tropico 4's run.  Now, with Tropico 5,  Kalypso/Haemimont are no longer on my radar, I don't care about their games.

That's okay.  I still have Tropico 4.


EDIT:  Some people have posted below with some very good arguments about where my review may be wrong.  I still feel my review stands, but if you are truly looking into whether you should spend your money on this game or not, it wouldn't hurt in reading the comments below for some very valid responses that may change your mind.

People say Tropico 4 is better, and while I agree to an extent, Tropico 5 was a better sequel to 4 than 4 was a sequel to 3. If you played and love Tropico 4, you'll probably enjoy Tropcio 5 IF you don't go in expecting that its Tropico 4 but with more features and stuff. Tropico 5 is a different game, and knows its a different game, forcing the player to approach things from a different perspective. You have some concern with researching things and moving onto the next era, building a sense of progression, and causing old tactics to create less profit, but allowing for new tactics to reek in even more cash. It should be noted that there could be more content building wise, but if you buy the game with all the DLC in a sale it would kind of remedy that. As far as the content in the game itself, it works, but there isn't really anything too interesting except for maybe a few exceptions, but the DLC adds some fun stuff like the Ministry of Truth, which is actually a fairly intersting building to use, and the water pack adds some interesting stuff. By themselves however, the DLC isn't really worth it except for like two of them, so I would recommend getting the bundle on a sale. Online with a friend can also be fun, though it does crash sometimes. The concept of racing to resources and being a thorn in your friend's side is fun.

tl;dr: It's not the same as Tropico 4, but it isn't trying to be and benefits from that. It's differences give it an identity, but you might be better buying the game with the dlc bundled on a sale if you need more content. Either way, it's a decent game. Online is decent with friends.

During the game's modern era, a certain bear-riding Russian leader, who isn't named, sent a large number of Russian immigrants to my island, which I stupidly accepted. Then he proceeded to invade my island under the justification of 'liberating the oppressed Russian minority in Tropico'.

10/10 for realism.

You may see a lot of reviews slamming this game for being "dumbed down" or overly simplified compared to previous titles, and to be honest they may not be entirely incorrect. However, what these people don't seem to grasp is that sometimes less is more. I will admit that Tropico 5 is certainly not a perfect game, nor is it even the best game in the series, but it still holds it own and should be considered by anybody who is a fan of the series or the genre.

I will start with the good, which there is plenty of. Tropico 5 has the most robust campaign of any Tropico game to date, with persistent islands that carry over from mission to mission and a new dynasty system that allows you to pass your legacy on to your offspring if you choose to. While the dynasty aspect could have been fleshed out a little more, it is still fun and finally gives you something to actually do with your off-shore account money (which is used to upgrade dynasty memebers). As usual the story to the campaign is wacky and goofy, and completely unbelievable, but that is all just part of the charm to Tropico. Tropico 5 also introduces a new era system where instead of always starting during the Cold War, you can now start as early as colonial times and work your way up through 4 eras to modern times. While not game-changing per say, this does add a nice touch to the game and a fresh way to play it. The voice acting throughout is solid and charming, the music is catchy as always, and the visual are superb. The color pallete is bright and cheerful, and the level of detail on some of the buildings is rather impressive when you zoom in. It should also be noted that as with most Kalypso games technically the game is great, it runs wonderfully and I have had zero crashes.

As I mentioned though, the game is not perfect I'm afraid. There are a couple of aspects of the game that have been simplified compared to old titles. For example, when setting the salary for a building instead of a slider that allowed you to set whatever dollar amount you wanted, there are just 5 pre-set payrates to choose from. Furthermore, while you can still set the pay from every building of that kind, you can't set it for all workers of that education. A slight annoyance, but still something that may detract from some and it also points to the larger issue with this game I think many have. This game is not City:Skylines, it is not Banished, nor is it even SimCity in terms of complexity. Tropico 5 is a largely streamlined experience that is intended to let you focus on the big picture without getting too caught up in micro-managing. Some people like this, some don't, which I get, but it should be noted Tropico games have always been like this so it really shouldn't be a shock that Tropico 5 continues the pattern. Another annoyance is the lack of content in this game. While the campaign is robust and plenty of maps are included for sandbox mode, it is frustrating to see buildings and concepts introduced in previous games either omitted or held out so that they can be introduced through over-priced DLC. That said, the base game as is still provides plenty to do and can be enjoyed without spending a penny on DLC. It should be noted though that the exact same argument could be made about the last game, as without the Modern Times expansion Tropico 4 was a little lacking in endgame content, so again this really is nothing new for the series.

All-in-all Tropico 5 is a really solid game. Not great, but also really not bad, and very much worth the only $40 it costs. I will admit that you may want to start with Tropico 4 (skip 3, 4 is just an upgraded version of it), and if you want a really good game that is completely different from the rest of the series play 2, but if you already have played these and are hungry for more or you just want to play the newest game, you will not regret this purchase. Also please note while my Steam account doesn't reflect it I have played every game in the series extensively, in particular 4 on the XBox 360, and while 2 actually remains my favorite 5 is right up there as well.

I'm a pretty big fan of games of this kind. I grew up playing the different versions of Sim City.

I'm also a big fan of Tropico 3 and 4, and bought this game on sale. Even on sale, I can't really recommend it and here's why:

They haven't fixed the most important problem.

If you've played Tropico extensively, like I have, you've run into the problem with road congestion. It has not been fixed. You must plan out very meticulously your road network from the VERY beginning of the game. Each subsequent story mission builds upon the progress you've made in previous missions. You use the same Island and city as before (there's 2 different islands, and thus two different cities). If you're not very careful, you'll end up like I did, 6 or 7 missions in without the means to really go in and rework everything, and it's not until that far in that the problem becomes very large and difficult to solve.

If you have a diverse economy, which is actually very easy to achieve in Tropico 5, it's not difficult to make quite a lot of money that can be invested into infrastructure, but the problem for me doesn't lie in having to rework infrastructure, it's that I'm working to circumvent poor coding (the road system I mentioned earlier) that has been in every Tropico game I've ever played.

Road management is a part of the game, I'm fully aware, but there is no management options. Tropicans will take the shortest route available. There are no one way street, or high volume highway like options. I can't do anything but build a singular type of road which nearly every building needs to be attached to. The only way to be completely efficient is to have EXTREMELY ugly circle roads that never connect to each other except by adjacent garages. Someone actually developed a circumvention system for Tropico 3 (which has persisted into 4 and 5 out of necessity). If you google "road congestion tropico", I'm sure you can find more information (if interested).

This Tropico is a little bit more challenging than the last ones in terms of Rebels and their threats. They attack much more often, and your army cannot be controlled beyond telling them which buildings you value the most. Rebels will attack from multiple points and your army sallies out of wherever you built your buildings. Since all you have is men on foot and eventually very slow tanks, the rebels will usually destroy several buildings before your army can even respond.

Rebels are also able to target your army squads while you are unable to control and choose targets for your own. What this means is that your army will be running to defend a certain building, and the rebels will follow along and continually fire at them while your army DOES NOT RETURN FIRE, and simply dies. It's EXTREMELY frustrating.

There's also a huge problem that persists with housing. 

As you might remember, people get old and retire and their income falls. There are children, unemployed and students as well. In Tropico 5, Houses now have budgets like employment buildings do. It is essentially the rent charge.

NO MATTER WHAT JOB PEOPLE HAVE, most of them will not live in a house because it is too expensive. Even if you've maximized the budget (and thus their pay) at their place of employment. You must lower the rent to a single point (out of a maximum of 5) in order to allow people to live there. YOU MUST turn on social security. Otherwise you will CONSTANTLY be attacked by rebels. YOU MUST do this for every housing building.

People will also not live in a building that is too far from where they work. Couples make a decision based upon both their work locations. If not satisfied with how close they live to work, they toss up a shack!

It is not uncommon to see shacks right beside housing units that are completely empty.

For some ungodly reason, Tenements lose housing value over time. There is no option to remedy this. This only way to circumvent is to completely destroy the building and replace it. It would have taken a few lines of code to add a renovate option, but no, they didn't do that. I wouldn't be surprised if it was in a DLC.

The graphics are improved, a lot of the mechanics of the game have been streamlined, but not fixed. There are improvements here, although the dynasty system is tacked on, stupid, and useless.

It feels like it's still Tropico. I don't know what it is that provides that feeling, the enjoyment of the game, and the music (I've always really enjoyed it) or the same bloody bugs that have persisted forever without attention.

I played Tropico 1, 2, 3, 4 and now the newest one. Let me give you some history for basing my opinion.

Tropico 1 was fun, innovative for its time, great ambience, nice enough music (a bit repetitive) and the missions were very straight foward, like a game in that era should be.

Tropico 2 was more of the same but with some great additions. The pirates theme, i guess, worked out really well. I enjoyed it for a long time before it got sort of pointless.

Tropico 3 is the first installment that you can call "the current generation" of the Tropico games. The controls and the GUI were terrible compared to T5, but in some ways, it was more rewarding to try and accomplish the side missions.

Tropico 4 was a massive improvement over T3. The best music so far, with a varied selection and you can't really get bored with them. The missions were OK, mostly made sense, which is good. Progression was very linear, in a satisfactory kind of way.

Now, TROPICO 5: the music has been toned down a little. No such quality or variety as found in the fourth game. 

The missions are basically life-savers that pop up in just the right time or a simple do-and-get-rewarded sort of scheme. The rewards are usually immigrants, cash or good standing with other nations. 

The graphics have improved a bit, yes, but it's not like you'll be playing this at the closest possible zoom all the time. Granted, when you do zoom in, the textures don't look washed out too badly and the characters and objects are a little bit higher poly than in T3 and 4.

The game is no longer THAT linear. You do end up being thrown back into the past to take revenge on your present-time enemies by sabotaging their past. That surprised me a bit and i liked it.

The whole technology progression thing deserves a compliment. This works in much the same way as Endless Space, which, in my view, is the very best technology tree found in a strategy game. It simply works nicely and gives you a good idea of the passage of time.

Overall, i would say this is, indeed, more of the same good old tropico, but it cannot be denied that it has been improved substantially. It does feel "new".

I give it a 8.5 out of 10. You really should try it if you like city builders in the likes of Patrician and Port Royale.
I would love to recommend this game. But the game update released 2 weeks ago made the game unplayable for myself and many many others. This still hasn't been fixed. Until then, I don't recommend.

Yep, it's another Tropico game...

There really isn't much more to say other than that.  It just feels lazy.  All your old favourite buildings return,  very few new ones.  DLC is silly expensive, customization is meh.  Save your money and go play one of the other tropicos.  Either 1,  or if you like roads,  3.

To elaborate.  

Building Variety - Tropico has never been big on this, but it's 2014.  Would it kill to have 2 models for a Bunhouse/house/etc?

Eras - These are esentially mini-goals.  If you fail to achieve them within the time limit,  you lose.  That's about it.  All they do is lock buildings from you,  making it harder to layout a good city -from the start-

Ships -  You get to own ships,  that sounds cool, and I really thought it was going to be like Tropico 2 managing pirate fleets.  But it's not.  You couldn't have any less interaction with them, No naming,  no colouring, and with each era, the ship just poofs into the next eras ship and keeps doing what it does.    Huge let down.

Mines - Ugly eyesores that just look silly when you upgrade them.   A mini Bagger 288 just sits there, and it's grosly undersized. 

Tanks - Yep, I'm gonna say this too.  The introduction of Tropico tanks.   They are T-34.  That's it. Every nation be it america,  soviets,  modern armour,, oh and of course Tropico,  all use the same model T-34.      

Bring Back TNT radio - I mean the Tropico 3 one, (but 4 is even better than this schlock).

Ultimately disappointing

I was a big fan of Tropico 3 and 4. This one is still playable, but just doesn't feel like it has the depth of the previous titles. Some of the additions I liked and thought were interesting changes, such as:

- You know have a ruling dynasty and you gain new family members as you go, with different abilities and bonuses

- You have different eras that you move through and different building available in each era. There is also a constitution with options in each area. This is how you control things like open or closed borders, conscription vs high quality military etc.

However, things I didn't like:

- It seems much harder to really get a picture of how your society is going. Little things like : previously in a school you could see all the students and click on them, now you just get '5/10 students' and you can't drill down on them. You can't seem to get a list of your whole population by education level, only the unemployed people. You can't see an individual persons needs anymore, just their ratings. It's harder to watch or track a single person. You can see thoughts, but not what they are currently doing, whereas they used to tell you they were going to the doctor, or to get food. You can't see how many people are using a garage or railway station. Lots of small features like this that they have removed make it really hard to diagnose problems, like whether people are able to commute effectively, or have enough services around them.

- Because of the above, when things go wrong, you often have no idea why. Why is the happiness rating high but my approval rating low? Why do I have so many of every type of entertainment building but the entertainment happiness is still low? Why do I have lots of teamsters but my factories are full on un picked-up goods? It's often hard to tell if it is something you are doing wrong, inconsistencies in the game or bugs. Why do I have so many homeless people who won't move into the housing I have built that is in a good location and appropriate for their wealth level? Why do I still have people listed as 'broke' when I have the social security edict turned on. Why is there a group protesting against my government, but when I click on them many have 85+ approval rating and happiness? What are they upset about? No idea.

All of that being said, the game is still fairly easy to complete, but for those like me that like to not just finish the mission but build the ultimate society in the process, it is so frustrating seeing things like a low approval rating due to homelessness when I have dozens of houses standing empty and other similar things. I ended up giving up because I just wasn't enjoying it any more.

For anyone new to the franchise, go and play 3 or 4, they are awesome.

Okay so....
If you are new to Tropico series, I'd suggest getting Tropico 4 instead as it's more "complete" compared to Tropico 5. Sure Tropico 5 has got interesting features like timeline where you start in Colonial Era and proceed to Modern Times, also more troops (now it's got fighter jets and tanks) so you have more variation in combat.

In term of controlling your city, Tropico 4 excels (in my opinion). In Tropico 5, they even remove ministers, so you can just issue any edicts you want. No more Immigration Office so you have to make amendment which once issued, you have to wait for really long time. Your character can visit places to "enhance" its efficiency and much more in Tropico 4. However, in Tropico 4, the military stuff is limited. You are only offered infantry and that's it, you can only fight the rebels and if someone wants to declare war on you it's an instant game over which is suck.

Player customization is limited as well in Tropico 5, you can't even name your character the way you want, the traits are not as many as Tropico 4. To replace this, Tropico 5 introduces "Dynasty". It's just your family, nothing special, you can choose one of the member to become the next president. For me, it's an upgrade, but the question is.... Why remove the freedom to customize your character?

What I like Tropico 5 the most is the multiplayer feature, unfortunately the game is not really crowded so you better have some friends playing with you. Because it's a race against time thanks to the timeline.

DLCs? I don't recommend it, it adds some features but you'll get bored easily. Besides, the DLCs are too many the price in total is just not worth it. The base game is actually enough.

Not a bad game, but minus the graphics, everything else is noticeably inferior compared to Tropico 4. This is despite having bought all the DLCs.
I'd recommend buying 4 instead of this one.

Tropico, as a city builder, is far too simplistic and heavily constrained in terms of space, due to the setting being on an island.
Plus, often towards the end game, it gets very easy to rack up too much money and not have anything much left to do.
However, as a single player campaign game, Tropico is great. So, its value, in my opinion, depends heavily on its story, humour, and voice acting.

That said, the story, humour, the voice acting, and the overall single player campaign is far superior in Tropico 4.
In that game, the character portraits and the voice acting had enough clues and character in them to be immediately understand what or who they represented. And what they said was actually funny and enjoyable.

In 5, it isn't the case. Spare the communist faction, when someone pops up in the story for the first time, it had me wondering who they were and where they'd fit in terms of the story line. Plus that, the jokes aren't as funny as 4, the voice acting isn't as good as 4, and so on.

Again, this isn't a bad game, but the previous game was far better than this. This one is rather mediocre.
I guess I must say I cannot recommend this one, since I must recommend you to buy Tropico 4 instead.

A good successor to Tropico 4, but with some missing features and less micromanagements. If you like city building games, I would recommend. Unlike most city builders, you can fail multiple ways. It has more innovation, challenging offers, and playstyles than Tropico 4.

Comparing to Tropico 4

Pros

Technology system and Era - Progress through eras to unlock new managers, buildings, and amendments. An awesome addition.

Constitution- allows you to run your nation. Form militias, create a free market, establish as theocracy, many different playstyles are available. A drawback is that some amendments are overpowered, and some are underpowered, but for the most part they are balanced.

Diplomacy- You have an embassy which you can manage diplomacy or from menu. In this game, you can get gifts from multiple nations. If you complete random delegation for a nation, you gain relations. Good relations can help you from an alliance, which can help your nation’s military (in addition to the gifts). If a nation hates you, you can defend against them unlike in Tropico 4.

Trade- You can gain trade routes through different means and are no longer just random. An example is building a lighthouse. This makes trade interesting as you get you more options. A slight downside to trade is that imports require trade routes and you can't manually adjust sliders for import quantity.

More challenging- I found this game to be more difficult. The economy in tropico 4 was a joke and was too easy to manage. In this game, careful management of managers, edicts, trade routes are required to create a good economy. Rebels are a greater problem in this game, and there is a new type of rebellion called uprising which is extremely difficult to fight, keeping you army loyal is important and you can no longer just give them a base and high wages to keep them loyal. 

Military and combat- They are a variety of military units and buildings, no more just bases and armories. Managing a military is simpler, no more getting generals and needing multiple armories for an army base, etc. All soldiers require high school, unless conscription is active, A fully employed army building gives you units in battle, it’s that simple.

Mixed

Tourism-  (I have changed my mind on tourism after playing playing a tourists sandbox) Tourism is viable, but there is only one real way to make it viable. Now there aren't variety in tourism entertainment types such as sightseeing or gambling, hotels can now only house a certain of tourism which I personally feel is a bad design decision. Perhaps the could have just have tourist preferences for a hotel type, but I degress. Tourist now come in through the distgusting industral dock on giant cruse ships (WHY!?). Tourism is actually viable if done correctely, in this game you must please multiple (20 of each class) tourist types in order to increase the # of tourists you can have (doesn't make much sense you can't specialize). You need to check tourist only to actually make good profit on entertainment buildings. Build banks with tourism upgrade and airports as well. Build luxury entertainment buildings for each tourist type to increase profit. For example, You can just spam night clubs for wealthy tourists and musuems for cultural tourists.  With this I was making 1-1.5 million a year.

Cons

Less micromanagement- You can no longer control wages and upkeep of buildings by a number, you now have a budget which you can raise which increase wages and upkeep. No more slave labor while running a strong economy anymore. Houses don't have rent controls; the quality of the house determines who can live there. Entertainment is also like this as well.

Absolute Military Dictatorship is less viable- The MD playstyle is less viable due to the way the military is in Tropico 5. The army bases don't provide healthcare or housing, so those needs must be meet through civilian buildings. Spamming Guard towers seems to be the best since tower guards can't rebel. This means you can't treat your military likes kings and the civilians like slaves, which is probably a good thing in some ways.

[strike]Worse Tourism. Tourism is now less viable and interesting.[/strike] 

Certain features removed- elections speeches, some factions, factions rebellions, monuments, avatar bio (replace with the overpowered but lackluster dynasty system).

It's the same Tropico we know and love but with a variety of new elements added to the core. Good fun, fantastic soundtrack and gorgeous graphics.

But I really do miss the faction leaders that conversed with you in Tropico 4, it let you know what needed fixing on the island and now the only indicator of shit hitting the fan is your almanac.. which really doesn't explain much. 

Also, the top left notification box tends to drag down the FPS rate whenever it appears. An option to disable  it and bring back the text notifications would be grand.

However this is still a great game and is worth the price of admission. 

EDIT - Lord Oaksworth can burn in hell.

The ethos of sequels back in the day used to be that they were bigger, better, and with more content. Unfortunatley the modern mindset seems to be that you can push out a minimal product at full price, and charge for "DLC" that should have been in the main game.
Every step taken by kalypso seems to be a step backwards. There are less buildings, less avenues for economy, less player agency. In tropico 4 you could entirely eschew certain areas of economy and still make it work. Want a industrial complex that sucks the minerals from the land for massive profit? No problem. Want to protect mother earth, build your economy by becoming a tourist trap, or an island vegas? Go for it! Do you want to create an atheist state, a complete theocracy, a communist regime, or a capitalist paradise? All do-able!
Not so with tropico 5. Make a single move that the people dont like, and you're done. in some cases there is no way to correct this (sign the wrong thing into your constitution, watch your approval tank. just watch, you can do nothing about it now.) its game over. You -must- build a church if you want to have any hope of making out of colonial era. You -must- build a mine if you want to have any economy at all.  While in tropico 4 you had to keep citizen happiness in mind, now it is the single driving factor of the entire game, and you will have to play it their way, not yours. Now that buildings are tied to eras, the game is completely homogonized. Every game is "A" leads to "B" leads to "C". you -must- start with farming, which -must- lead to industrialization, with no options for tourism or even entertainment until the right era.
And the DLC that is planned for this game is beyond insulting. there are so many features from tropico 4 that were taken out so that they could be resold in bits and pieces. Remove jails and make the game activley punish you for trying to deal with criminals. Oh but dont worry, there is a prison DLC coming out that you can buy. It reminds me of a mobile free to play game, only i unfortunatley payed money for it.
Tropico 4 was one of my favotire city building games, with many interesting mechanics and conecpts that couldn't be found elsewhere. Tropico 5 is an incredible disappointment, i cant recomend anyone buy this game. To echo many other sentiments, buy tropico 4 if you are interested in it.

Unfortunately I just can't recommend this game as much as I would have loved to. 

When I first played it, it was a nice refresh and continuation of Tropico 4. As I played it more, I found more and more problems with the game. The fighting, the buildings, the overlays (pre building placement and post placement), rebels, population cap, to name a few. I'll summarise these quickly:

The fighting: Essentially, its build a huge military or be wiped out. Once rebels appear, if they break through your military (which they will as they are OP most of the time), they head straight to the palace and game over. Your military doesn't respawn, you cannot rebuild military buildings either. Even if your barracks refill with 8 troopers, they won't go and fight the rebels attacking the palace. Totally ridiculous and to me, its a game breaker.

The buildings: Only apartments have 'variations' and even then they look pretty much the same. Throughout the eras, the building all look the same, modern housing in colonial periods. Really? There needs to be much more variation in models. As it stands now, its bland. There are buildings missing too that should really be in there. Since when did a police station act as a fire station? Seems lazy. Modern tanks appearing in the cold war era too.

Overlays: When you place buildings that say 'Affects nearby plantations' or 'Generates funds off nearby housing', there is nothing to say how far this radius is. You have no idea what it will affect until its placed and built. These buildings often cost alot to make and many times where you place can be a total waste of resources. For a modern 2014 game, this is not acceptable to me. Kalypso merely say its meant to be this way and is fine, and then point about overlays in the Almanac which are irrelivent to the point raised to them. There is nothing to say what the radius is of any building. This is a poor effort.

Rebels - too common, too OP. Doesn't give the feeling of a dictatorship game at all. Even on high happiness (some people have rebel attacks at 100 happiness). There are no real reasons for rebels alot of the time, and to many, its unknown why they are attacking since everyone is happy. I loved Tropico 4 to an unhealthy degree of obsession. It was the first Tropico game I had played and I couldn't wait for Tropico 5. Like most I've been disappointed with the changes made. They aren't bad, they just don't work too well. Tropico 4 was a waiting game, you had to wait for buildings to be finished. Coop is pretty pointless because it's just the base game with someone else on the island taking up space and resources. It's still just as boring and waiting around for your citizens to be happy enough to advance to the next era.

My final thought is that this game should be good, possibily even really good. But cutting out content for future DLCs and expansions makes me not want to invest any more time with Tropico 5 when the base contains so little.

El Presidenté deserves more.

STOP.  If you already own Tropico 4 you probably don't need this game and it will likely frustrate you.  I'm writing this review in the days after release so my gameplay time of Tropico 5 has admitedly been limited.  That said, I've played the Tropico series since the original back in the early 2000's.  I get that changes need to be made to keep the game relevant, but in my opinion Tropico 5 changed largely in the wrong direction.  However, if you're new to the series, you'll enjoy this game for what it has to offer.  Here's my initial breakdown.

Pros:

Beautifully redesigned buildings, everything just seems to fit together nicely when you're trying to cram a lot of buildings into one space.
The dynasty member function seems like a possible plus (haven't really fleshed that out yet).
I like the concept of having manager's in buildings, but it's not clear how they contribute to the overall expense of the building.
I like some of the new edicts like charging for healthcare!  Finally those lazy peasants will pay or die.
The addition of tanks adds a layer of badassery and battling rebels/other nations is more engaging.

Cons:

Can't set the exact wage for a worker anymore (it's done in an overarching budget system, so you set a budget for a building which somehow encompasses a salary for the worker and operating costs for the building).  You want to pay your farmers more than your doctors?  Sorry, can't do that...
You also can't set the exact amount for rent anymore.
The above two issues make it hard to become an uber-capitalist dictator.  I know it sounds ridiculous but they've dumbed down the economic system so much it's actually complicated.
Customizing your character is gone.  I don't care so much about what they look like, but who thought an astronaut suit should be 1 of the 5 outfits you get to choose?  I'm more upset you can't select negative and positive traits to create a more in depth character.  I always liked choosing flatulence even though the palace guards got double pay...
Am I missing the plants and shrubbery somwhere?  You basically have a large park and a small park, that's it.  No single palm trees to meticulously line your roadways...  Statues meant to glorify El Presidente's and intimidate your opponents are non-existent.
You have to pay to explore your island now which seems pointless.
Options like "paper plates" and "cloth napkins" that used to affect the quality of a restaurant are no longer options.  You adjust the budget of the building now to change service, but that raises the worker's wages.  What if I want to increase quality without raising wages...  
El Presidente is pretty much useless.  He can't help rush construction or join in fighting the rebels like in previous games.  No option to sway election with speeches either.
Building progression through research/time feels poorly developed and arbitrary.  You earn research points through libraries and observatories which give you tech upgrades for different buildings.  Unfortunately, you can only build tenaments and country houses at the beginning so if you want to upgrade your citizens to apartments to improve housing quaility you have to wait until the Cold War era (and then destroy all your previous housing and try to make the apartments fit into your city layout).  I wasn't a fan of Tropico 4's purchasing blueprints, but I think it works better than this option.
You can no longer see who is actually visiting a restaurant, pub, doctor's office, etc.  You're just given a "number of visitors".
Searching in the almanac is painful.  All I want to do is find the least happy person and execute them, but you can't search by that.  You can find the person with the lowest approval rating, but they're not necessarily the most unhappy.
I know this is knit-picking, but I liked when you purchased a building upgrade in previous Tropico's, the physical improvement would appear (i.e. skylights in the cigar factory).  There's no visual changes on the buildings when upgrading now.
You can't toggle a dock to accept "tourists only" so I keep having my teamsters dropping export resources at the dock in my tourist area.  I don't want stinking peasants mixing with the upper echelons of society. 
Only a handful of island maps to play.
One of the biggest negatives for me is the overall lack of buildings (where's the gourmet restaurant??? or El Presidente's childhood museum?).  I assume this is so we can be sold the inevitable expansion packs.

Suggestions:

The ability to choose the placement of our palace and dock at the outset of a sandbox game would be nice. 
Consider reverting back to SOME, not all, of the core game designs from previous versions.  My big ones would be charging specific amount of rent and setting worker's wages (please change this back).
True roundabouts would be great for improving traffic flow.

Even with all the above, I'll still play it because I absolutely love Tropico, but just a lackluster delivery compared to past game versions.  Overall rating from me would be a 6 out of 10.
I love being a dictator and violating human rights for my own personal benefit.

Too many simple quality-of-life features are hidden behind DLC paywalls.  Just sell the game for the price it is, do not combine nickel-and-dime with bait-and-switch.  I'd have bought this for the full price if honestly marketed from the beginning.  But the business model of "get them hooked on a stripped-down version and then charge for simple features" is bad business ethics.  And devs' responses in community questions are some "Don't you guys have phones" tone-deaf behavior.

It seems they learned from this mistake, because the 6th installment does not have these problems to nearly this degree.

So, I've seen this game get a lott of guff for not being like Tropico 4. Now, having owned both, I can truthfully say; that's not necessarily a bad thing. Should you get T4? Yes, it's a great game. Should you get T5? Yeah, it's also a great game. Why? Because they're both their own games. You'll find, as a gamer, you'll enjoy things more if you can appreciate what makes them unique instead of looking for new graphics for the same old game. 

TL;DR: Don't listen to the haters, El Presidente; your people need you. (Especially on sale)

This game takes you through Eras, not just a one and done Building Cycle, Governing Factions and Trade fluxuations. I swear, T4 was almost too easy with its Factions setup (at least for me). From foreign powers to local politics each Era has its own flavor of personal dealings, edicts and the like. 

The game has controller support. Yeah, I like that. I stopped trying to create Powerpoint presentations on my PS4 and likewise stopped trying to play every game on my computer with a mouse and keyboard. It's the little things I appreciate. Like also how the different buildings have their own levels of investment to affect their production levels and managers you can hire to offer little bonuses. 

The way the farms and mines lay out are much more user friendly in T5 as well. It's almost seamless checking between variant crops and ranches to their respective areas to see what would fit where best. The plantations show an accurate area usage for your consideration when placing them and the overall feel of the building options seems fluid. 

I personally enjoy the little stamps as the icons, I find that to be fitting to the theme of Tropico. I have no trouble knowing where the different sets of buildings are and their skins (especially as how they partain to the various eras) are vibrant and well drawn.

There's a fog of war on this game. Interesting use, you can send expeditions out there to find out what lies beyond. I like it. I like the exploration value instead of taking 5 minutes at the start of a map to see where literally everything is. There's more gaming aspects to this Tropico than there was to the last, more ways to enjoy the game besides finding new ways to make the same winning combination of goods and policies. 

Basically, if you wanna hate on a game, you can find a reason. Me? I'm El Presidente, I have no time for such plebieans.  Game on, fellow Dictators!

Ok, so here we are. I bought this game years ago and as you can see, I have all the DLC, played through all 3 campaigns and got well over 200 hours in. So why the no?

Simple. This game is worse than Tropico 4 in almost every way. Don't get me wrong, T5 isn't a bad game, but when compared to T4... yeah. I own T4 on DVD, got none of the DLC and still, it feels so much better. While Tropico 3 felt more like a 3d rehash of T1, Tropico 4 became the one i would consider the best of the series, thou I have not played T6, but that one's giving me major T5 vibes so don't bet on it.

So, what went wrong? For starters, the happiness system has become a mess. No matter how many health buildings you construct, people seem to always die in droves. Well, until you advance in the ages and can build a hospital, which, surprise surprise, your city layout has no room for because you did not know that you should leave a spot because this game works on a grid system that leaves ugly green spots littered across the city because the building foundations don't line up.
Which leads into point two, the age system. While a good idea on paper, it just locks necessary edicts and crucial buildings behind research and artificial barriers. This results in big cities complaining about religion, but he, can't build one of the oldest buildings in medieval history without advancing first, something that should be constructible in the colonial age. Because cathedrals did not exist until the cold war.

Other aspects were also dumbed down. Back in T4, you got a special event for every faction crisis. Here you get... nothing. Absolutely nothing. Speaking of the story.
In T4 you get a conspiracy about the murder of the president as well as a cast of major rivals you tear down one by one. In T5 you get... the Illuminati and time travel. Look, at least we still have Penultimo and his antics. Which leads into the two islands problem.

During the campaign you always have to choose from one of two islands between missions. This is arse. Why? Simple, you can have a perfect island and then you switch and nothing works anymore on the new island as you struggle to get that one working as there has been an age change and now the people demand things you can't buy as new factions have popped up that put the happiness below 50 as you loose the first elections without any fault of your own.

And then several components were removed. A detailed backstory for your presidente with weaknesses, a path to power and an extensive customizations system. So what did T4 get? Backstories are ripped out, everything worse and you CANNOT EVEN NAME YOUR PRESIDENT. Let that sink in.
You want to create a stalin look-a-like? Well, tough shite, all you have is a guy name Juan because we have a SELECTION of first names and you gonna like it. Gone are speeches to make promises for your next term or directly ordering the president to help with battle or construction. Now you got a family of soulless husks.

All of this makes Tropico 5 not a bad game. But compared to Tropico 4 it's just not worth it. Buy 4 instead.

I find Tropico 5 to be in two places.  Yes, I like it.  It's another Tropico game.  Good job, well done, now shut up and take my money and let me get that sweet sweet fix.


The changes to Tropico from previous games include the introduction of eras, and such. The game is divided into four eras, you have to maneuver your island through, and as you do, you unlock new research, can issue new edicts, and can build new buildings.  But the result is that the eras lock your choices, and thus create a similar game each time.  For example, in previous editions of Tropico, you could build a tourist paradise very early in the game as a way to make money.  In this game, you have no tourist things unlocked until the 3rd era, and many of the better ones aren't until the 4th.  The result is that you really are unable to tap into tourist stuff until much later in the game.  And that is the same in each game, in part, because there aren't as many things do use.

There are fewer things to build - fewer homes to live, fewer recreational options, and more.  There are also fewer options with the things you do have.  In previous editions of the game, I could build a media outlet like a Newspaper and then choose if I wanted it to help a certain faction or be a propaganda arm for my state.  No longer.  I have no options any more with that. Meanwhile, gone are things like the Immigrant Office that I could use to determine my immigrant policy.  The citizenship options aren't nearly as robust in the Constitution.  Gone is the ability to choose multiple things to distinguish about your character.  I loved the traits, abilities and limitations you had to have earlier, and that really helped to distinguish the game.  When one character began with a free hotel, that was something. Another would have a free Cement Factory and a third a great relationship with the various nations.  They encouraged different play throughs.  But in this?  Just one trait that's almost nonexistant in gameplay.  

A few other things are missing that I think were pretty cool in older games, like El Presidente's Childhood Home, the Movie Theater,  and the above-mentioned Cement Factory that would increase your build speed.  Little bonuses like that were great!  And getting something like the Childhood Home is awesome.   It drips flavor.

I love the Constitutional addition.  It allows you to control your policies much better (save for immigration) and in many ways where you couldn't before.  I also beeline for the Constitutional updates in each era in terms of research so I can add more policies to my nation.  And there are times I'm not really sure which policy to implement.  I've had great success with both planned economy and free market.  I think Theocracy is very strong compared to Secular State or Atheist State.  


So that is an addition that is so good that once you play with it, you never want to go back!

Another great addition s the trade system. I like building trade options and purchasing things my island needs or selling steel behind the back of my dopey EU allies to Russia who pays more money.  That's good stuff. 

I do think the Fog of War is an inconvenience and just an early game money sink.  It's an island, not a continent.  You don't need to explore it to find out what is in your mines or to make a road.  And later, you'll get a research (compass) that removes anything left.  I don't like FOW for this game at all. It's like adding a FOW to SimCity and you have to explore the areas before you build in them.  Would that make a lick of sense?

Multiplayer?  So awesome!

I do like some of the additions in the DLC, but they are uneven value. The one that gives you a creamery for your milk is, by far, the best of the one note stuff.  All of the spy and military line from Espionage is really powerful, and the water options are good as well.  Every a single island of mine has at least one creamery, and multiple buildings from the other options.  But some, like the Giant Ray Gun, just do nothing.  You are not building anything in those.

It is nice to have a sub, drones, and even an aircraft carrier for defense though.  I was attacked by the US recently, and just barely lost.  But you can not have commandos and tanks and such to help defend, and I like Tropico's moves in that direction.

It also makes me laugh to see rebels crushed by my tanks.

So overall, I get T5 a thumbs up.  That is qualified into two camps.  It errs.  It makes some mistakes.  It's the worst entry in the series by far.  For the first time in my life, I am not going to auto-buy Tropico 6 next year when it's released, because I don't like the potential downward progression this game series has.  And the plot in the scenarios and events have gone into bizarre territories. Time travel? Death rays? Clones?  This is not a James Bond film, and if I wanted to play as the villain in one, I'd go with Evil Genius, not Tropico.  

But the game works.  It makes me smile.  I stayed up late until 4:00 am a few days ago playing it.  It's still recommended!

In the words of Penultimo: I am so furious!
If I wanted to play a military strategy, I wouldn't play Tropico. The allure of the game was, in the first place, being able to develop an economy while ignoring (And profiting! from) world wars and such. and now, i have to siphon the money in military bases, barracks, alliances, and still I get two simultaneous invasion forces on my shores, impossible to defeat unless I have ludicrous ammount of firepower myself. And it's not the firepower I want when I play Tropico. I want humor, sleezy diplomacy and pina coladas.
Not to mention the lack of ammount of zoom that existed in previous incarnations of the game,and lack of info about buildings.
I'ma lover, not a fighter. Let's hope the next incarnaton of Tropico will have less tanks and more casinos

I'm recommending this game for one reason: Multiplayer

Tropico 5 nailed the multiplayer aspect.
Being able to play alongside my friends is the reason I love this game.
It's the best multiplayer city building game out there. I have not come across any other like this.

Advice: Spam sugar plantations and rum distillaries.

What's with all the hate lately. This game was released in 2014 and I still play it in 2019. It's an amazing game. The publisher has even reduced the price accordingly with the games age. This is one of those games I happily bought even after "playing a friends backup copy" many hours.

Firstly, let me make it clear that this is by no means a bad game. If you had no previous experience of Tropico and someone gave you this for free you'd probably be very happy. Unfortunately, comapred to the (cheaper) Tropico 4 this is just seems inferior in so many ways. The storyline is the usual entertaining farce and the new era system works pretty well in that you have a different feel for each time period in terms of interaction with foerign powers. However, it also feels like it's not been totally intergrated (the Colonial era has citizens in the garb of the Pilgrim Fathers but with standard asphalt roads). There's also a new trade system but it just seems different rather than better. The  biggest bugbear is the feeling that it's all been dumbed down. There are fewer micro management options, the almanac has less information (especially regarding politics) and there seem to be less building options. This means that often there feels like there is nothing much to do once a mission gets going and often it's just a case of letting the clock run down, occasionally throwing down some random buildings to fulfil a quest. With Tropico 4 I remember being chopping at the bit to get onto the next mission. After 10 hours of Tropico 5 I'm afraid I'm just a bit bored.

Pretty game. Still has some of the charm of old Tropicos and makes some improvements, as one would hope. The continuous islands, while a bit repetitive, are nice because the game builds on itself and you don't feel like you lose everything with every new level.

Buuuut since you can't unlock certain buildings until different eras in the game, people are just dying and unhappy and there's virtually nothing you can do about it. So you're trying to go about your business and build an economy while tredging through uprising after coup every (no exageration) 3-5 minutes. Really takes away from the experience. And they have changed the employment and payment systems so you have less control than ever over those aspects, which adds to people's eager hatred and takes away from the management feel.

I wanted to like this game. It still has some promise, but overall, disappointed. I got it on sale... I would recommend doing the same if you still want to pick it up.

Another addition to the Tropico series. I own every single Tropico game out there and so I'm acquainted with the game. People may disagree with this review yet in comparison of the other Tropico games I don't really feel this game adds a whole lot. While Tropico 5 ushers in new options, the metrics the game offers you by way of info for economics is sorely lacking. Overall, this game takes a more casual approach towards the series with a campaign that is poorly written. For those who prefer growing your economy, enjoying a mixed economy while trying to appease facitons, perhaps stick with Tropico 4 because the constant barrage of crises faced when playing Tropico 5 turned me off.

Pros:

-Tropico 5 ushers in new options and concepts not found in the previous series. Things like buildings auto-demolishing themselves once they've outlived their usefulness (like a logging mill) is a welcome change to manage buildings. 
-The addition of newer buildings adds greater variety to the landscape.
- The introduction of research points generated from a library is interesting and allows you to research a variety of upgrades.
- You can upgrade certain buildings in order to enhance certain aspects like productivity of the buildngs.
- You can establish trade routes now through the docks.
- You can now hire managers with speficic traits to run specific buildings with those traits benefiting the buildings.
- New buildings offered (i.e. Inquisition) offer the chance for you to carry out additional activities like label people heretics, etc.

Cons:

- The campaign is frankly confusing and poorly laid out. With the introduction of a dynasty whereby you can choose to create different members of your ruling family, it makes for too many choices in what should otherwise a simply process of going from one campaign to the next. I would have much preferred a more simple layout to show progress with the campaign.
- Second, after having purchased and fought for your independence, you find yourself governing another island and yet the same Crown representative is bugging you with requests and you have to work again towards independence. The campaign should progress with different goals which makes this tedious.
- There is no fluidity from one campaign to the next. Once you finish one objective, you've back in the main menu, whereby you save, and then choose another island. Why not simply transition right away?
- The Crown constantly asking you for money to leave you alone is annoying and takes place way too early in the game. It takes away from growing your economy and instead you're left dishing out money left right and centre. I get that the devs wanted to make the game more challenging but frankly there are so many frequent interruptions it becomes annoying.
- The Crown will let you know that your colony is doing poorly compared to other colonies and so what does it do? It penalizes you with a tax of 10k that allows you to continue playing but puts you further into debt. DUH. Penalize me for doing badly by putting me further into the hole? 
- In certain missions, the crown will penalize you for doing poorly but then 5 minutes send you 6k. Wtf?
- In another campaign the crown will hit you with a real estate tax and then two seconds later you'll get a disbursement of 6k. 
- The almanac does a piss poor job of expanding on important aspects of your government. You cannot expand bullets under the Trade option with Economy to expand your revenue and expenses. Hell, even in Tropico 3, the GUI for info about the island was boring but it still allowed you greater freedom in clicking on certain metrics and being able to see immediately where you were hurting.
- Unlike Tropico 4, setting wages for jobs is confusing. Instead of a "wages" option you have a budget set for the building. Budget for what? Maintenance or wages?

Conclusion: Tropico 5 offers a variety of improvements in certain areas and upgrades in its buildings but for Tropico aficionados like myself, I found the game hampered by a poorly written and confusing campaign that make playing the game. It's clear that the game takes on greater economic challenges that make please some people. There is fun to be had while you play a campaign and it is clear that the devs have modernized the series but frankly I feel the game is hamstrung by the campaign. If you are a hardcore fan you may be disappointed and choose instead to stick to Tropico 4, but if this on sale it may be worth it. 

Oh, and one more thing: by the way, Haemimont Games: if I buy a digital game, I don't expect to have to register an account with you to download "updates" and get passed your stupid fucking nag screen. It is fucking annoying and completely useless. Get rid of the fucking piece of shit nag screen.

This is the first Tropico game I haven't enjoyed. You seem to spend the entre game fire fighting and the campaign is just freaking annoying. I'd rather have realistic economic goals for my island than some far fetched plot about the end of the world. You end up just not caring. It of course retains it's typical humour but really goes overkill to a point that any characters in the games are incredibly unlikable. Even your own president. 

There's a wide array of buildings to choose from and I really liked the progression through the era's - Colonial through to Present day but the games campaign revolves around heavy military usage, yet you once again lack real control over your troops. It's highly annoying to watch them act consistently like brainless turds during an invasion or rebel uprising.

Furthermore, the game has issues with the staffing of your buildings, as your island becomes ever more populous people seem unwilling to ever work in your manufacturing plants meaning they stand there empty most of the time. Frustrating is not the word. Not to mention that mining resources run out far too quickly meaning you can miss targets in game since you son't actually have anymore of that resource to mine. 

And finally, the targets are boring as hell. Given that there's now 5 countries (Yes, Europe isn't a country but whatever) you can negotiate with, why do they want the same things all of the time.


I did enjoy playing Tropico at times, but it is a seriously lazy game. If the developers had spent more time balancing the above issues and ditching the cheesy puns that occur every 5 seconds then, maybe just maybe, i'd recommend it to you. Only ever buy on a Sale at a very generous rate.

Tropico 5 is I assume the 5th entry in the Tropico series, this time introducing a new "dynasty system" where you play throughout various eras. You'll start out in the colonial, then the world wars (yeah, it's a jump), the cold war, and then the modern era. I would say each era has their own "mechanics", but it's more of a new coat of paint, where you just get upgraded buildings and the attackers get a skin change. This isn't the say the era changes aren't fun, as going from the first to the last is engaging and really makes you feel like you made a lot of progress. The core of the game is still the same, you build on an island, research technologies to unlock more buildings, make policies, and try to stay in power. There's a bit more emphasis on combat in this one, at least in the campaign, as you have new military units and frequently fight other countries instead of just rebels. The combat is simplistic and you don't have much control of it, purely depending on the amount of units you have on your island. Still, choosing sides during the eras can make you feel like you're actually "involved" in world diplomacy as you increase your population and try to keep your people happy. You may find yourself struggling sometimes as you don't know why you're losing so much money, or why your people hate you so much. At the core of the game though, it's just you producing resources and trading (eventually being forced to as there's a limited amount of raw materials). It should be noted all trading is done automatically, although you can pick focuses to get more money.

There's no question that some eras are weaker than others, with the colonial seemingly just slapped in there to make it an even 4. The campaign's story is actually pretty funny, although you might get annoyed that you have to rotate between two maps (therefore being forced to repeat what you did already). The missions tend to be similar to each other and some tend to over emphasize on the weak combat system, causing you to focus on building a military instead of actually developing your island. It's unfortunate that the building variety is severely lacking, even if you have all the DLC, and it's just boring to have the same buildings repeat over and over again. The elections are also so arbitrary it too acts as an annoyance, and there's no special mechanics to it or even events. It's further unfortunate that the DLC seems to lock content off of what was supposed to be in the main game, forcing you to want to buy some of them in order to make the main game less tedious. There's strangely a large amount of missions you can take that keep you from just focusing on building, although they will eventually become tedious. Even with that though, most of them do not add enough for the price. Overall, with the expanded diplomacy options and era mechanics, I'd say this would be a decent Tropico game for you to try out.

The new radio voice, Lulu or what her name is, is infuriating and annoying and makes me genuinely miss Sunny Flowers, of all people. Sunny at least had redeeming qualities and was funny. I also miss giving election speeches. Elections just happen, and you can drop 20 % in approval by just having another wave of unstoppable immigrants who arrive poor and homeless. Even with your constitution set to "wealthy citizens vote". My borders are a figment of my imagination. No matter what option I take, I get waves and waves of uneducated schmucks. At least it doesn't seem to bother the nationalists, if they exist. I have not seen any tasks relating to their happiness and I finished the campaign and played a bunch of sandbox games.

Foreign powers constantly ask for stupid things, be it researching techs years away from what I can reasonably research or wanting me to export things I don't have, i.e. 10.000 milk when my entire island is at best 'yellow' efficiency for ranches.

The trade routes aren't the worst thing ever, but they are often not as flexible as they need to be. If I start importing the milk an ignorant foreign power demanded, I may sometimes only have an import offer lasting 15 years. So I either take it and block my ship for 15 years, or I assign it to a new route halfway through and get spammed with reminders that a trade route has no active ships.

The military, while having a good variety of new buildings, is uncontrollable. All I can do is litter my island with military buildings and hope the idiots dance in the right direction if I'm being attacked. The only unit I can tell where to go are scouting troops. Out of combat. It is a real improvement to have the Conscription option that allows uneducated people to become soldiers, which can help greatly in later eras. Most jobs will be High School and the neverending floods of immigrants are at least useful for a mass over class strategy of defense.

The most infuriating thing is wealth levels. Citizens will be broke, poor, well-off, rich or filthy rich. And anything below their level - which is entirely tied to their job - will be 'beneath' them. If you lower rent on a 'rich' category mansion to make it affordable for 'well-off' citizens, the rich will rather sit in a shack next to it than move into an unoccupied spot. If you 'upgrade' (downgrade) your Opera House to allow non-wealthy citizens in, the wealthy will shun it and whine about lacking entertainment.
Especially in the early eras, the options for entertainment are limited to three buildings only. And speaking of limited options, the entertainment category isn't the only one suffering from it. There are new Raw Materials (i.e. ranches have cattle, llamas, pigs and goats), as mentioned above new military buildings and a variety of new tourism buildings (mainly hotel types). Residental, on the other hand, all looks the same. Building the same tenements and apartments over and over again makes for pretty boring islands.

Mechanically, it is certainly interesting to have a Constitution (if the options worked as described) and to continue on the same island through all game eras (or better, 2 islands, as you switch between them in the campaign). As interesting as the idea is, as poor is the execution. If you made a mistake in the previous mission, there is no way to fix it. Events like disasters are apparently scripted and you can find yourself in no way out scenarios. There is no ability to 'restart', unless you make a new save file at the start of every mission. Even then, you're stuck with the old progress and the current status might be beyond repair.

I haven't tried multiplayer, but after reading it puts both players on the same island, I have no desire to try it either. What is the point of building on the same island, with the same resources? I was hoping for the option to have another player take a second island, to trade resources, maybe ship citizens or troops over in times of need, navigating diplomacy when each allied with a different superpower, competing for tourists, something like that. But nope, just trying to fit 2 cities on the same island for no reason.

Tropico 5 is a new proposition for the series and the results are quite mixed. Right off the bat, it is visible how this game is the product of a decision by committee, as it is so bland in every way. All the mechanics have been simplified and even the music, the staple of the series, is visibly more generic and inferior to its predecessor. The abandonment of classic systems in favor of completely new ones was an unfortunate decision. The Dynasty system and multiplayer were not well implemented. There are also bugs and bad design. Overall this game is very dull and mediocre.

While the gameplay is not particularly difficult, it is punishing. The new economy is broken and ineffective, with the country's finances struggling continuously and constantly falling into spirals of debt that force restarts. Profitable raw material production stalls when industrializing because the factories keep losing money; with the economical fleet of clay of your ever floundering system collapsing onto itself. There is also a continuous bleeding of population that forces you into debt and then into starvation. Demolishing half of your city is a better option to balance the budget. Tourism, always the poor cousin in the series, is simply not a viable option. There is also an inconsequential tech tree. The trade route system was a solution looking for a problem. The multiplayer is a good idea but not fun, with all 2-4 players just governing their islands independently.

The new budget system is an affront to God. You no longer control the salaries of your workers. Rather, you just fix a collective budget that decides the works' social class. It is stiff and takes away the president's capacity to rule its people. The game becomes streamlined and predictable. With such time spent in debt just looking at the screen, there is not much "city-building" in the city builder. The factions were eliminated in practice, with no faction leaders to address, thus nullifying internal politics in the game; the very essence of Tropico. Battles used to be events but now combat flares up for no reason, and it just becomes background noise after a while.

As for the era system, you start at the 19th century as a colony and work your way up to the modern era. This new system locks buildings and edits - which is not fun. The first era is more of a chore than anything else. There are few building options and the gameplay is limited to desperatly surviving with your mandate through continuous demands by the Crown. It is no wonder that every multiplayer game starts in the World Wars. Another problem is how the art doesn't convey the changing eras very well: Soldiers jump from muskets to M16 rifles and green uniforms from the 1960s. At the World Wars, Latin American militaries would have Pickelhaube and Adrian helmets. Those would have been fine additions to the style of the game. And another thing: the game believes Tropico is a British colony, not Spanish!

The characters are few and have far less charisma. Penultimo is the best, as your most loyal follower would be. Everybody else is new. Adriana is the most promising, but underused. She is cute with her short hair and iron resolve, but she appears only in the campaign. Veneno is the worst, and she speaks slowly and in monotone. One can see that most of the effort was put into the hilarious writing, with jokes and pop culture references abounding. The radio operator Lulu is less funny than Sunny, but miles better than Juanito. However, Lulu gets interrupted all the time with people jumping at your face with repetitive problems.

The Dinasty system is were the game fails completely. You no longer control El Presidente around the island. Instead, you get 6 generic family members (quite often very ugly) in attires of limited stock walking around like any other citizen. And that is the great tragedy of Tropico 5: the loss of identity. The connection of El Presidente and the Tropican is what makes this franchise special. Now it is all numbers and impersonal data. You can't even zoom the island properly and everybody is just so tiny you can't even see them in detail. Specific characteristics of the professions were also eliminated. The music is bland and forgettable.

Overall, the gameplay is repetitive and gets boring quickly. So... in the proud history of the Tropican nation, Tropico 5 is best forgotten.

I love Tropico 3, and 4 and I wanted to love Tropico 5, but  I just can't.

Tropico 5 feels like a city builder that forgot it was supposed to be fun. Tropico 3 and 4 let you build your island your way. Tropico 5 constantly interrupts you with forced tasks that drag you through a rigid checklist instead of letting you play.

Every mission pushes you into a sequence of mandatory objectives that you cannot ignore. You are not shaping your island. You are following instructions. The game stops you from experimenting or developing your own strategy. It feels like you are doing chores instead of running a dictatorship. This is one of the most baffling decisions. Tropico 3 and 4 let you replay missions, skip ones you disliked, or revisit your favourites. Tropico 5 locks you into a linear campaign with no mission select at all. If you get stuck or want to try a different approach, you are forced to replay the entire chain. It is restrictive and frustrating.

Early Invasions Are Miserable!!!!

The pacing is completely off. You barely have an economy, your population is starving, and you have two guard towers. Suddenly a global superpower decides to invade your tiny island. You have no army, no money, and no chance. It is not challenging in a fun way. It is just bad design that punishes you before you have any tools to respond.

El Presidente Loses All Personality. In Tropico 3 and 4, El Presidente felt like an actual character. You could give speeches, visit workplaces, and interact with your island in ways that added charm and humour. Tropico 5 removes all of that. No speeches. No workplace visits. No presence. El Presidente becomes a portrait in a menu instead of the heart of the game.

Don't bother, just play Tropico 4.

I loved Tropico 4, rule your own country, make your economy rise, satisfy your people, execute those in your way, piss off foreign countries and wave your nuke around to prevent them from invading. These are just some of the things you can do in the previous game and are still present in 5. 

But Tropico 5 changed in different ways, military became much more critical, forces are stronger thus stronger defense is required. Trade routes can be chosen and relations with foreign countries' relations affect these. You progress through time and things change even more than Modern Times DLC in 4. Housing is more interconnected with job salary and sometimes you experience problems but don't know the details until you see a detail that changes your prespective. The game provides a bigger mirror to the perspective of a dictator, things need to be watched more often and closely, you must be prepared and at the same time be able to adapt to the situations you must be watchful of such as civil unrest and the end of WWII.

Everything got more difficult, more complex, in some cases worse than 4, I miss the old Penultimo, I missing allowing no rent to all residentials, I miss the diverse set of characters and more. But 5 had some things I really liked, the campaign was something I didn't expect and loved, the fact that you make your island grow and don't abandon it at the end of the episode makes you see how difficult it gets to run a country the longer it stays alive. You have multiplayer (which sucked earlier on until some updates) where you cooperate or kill each other with armies and resources. Military played a bigger role, both a good thing and a bad thing because I didn't give a damn about it til 5.

Bottomline, Tropico 5 is like a more difficult version of 4, things need to be watched more often as the threat level of everything got more critical such as rebels, civil unrest and pirates and the campaign requires you to realize that you are NOT going to abandon your country and ALL problems you experience now WILL happen into the future unless YOU fix it while you can. Tropico 5 is a great game and I value it as I value 4 but in different ways.

If you value a bigger challenge, a more complex way of playing it, a chance to compete with other dictators (heads up, few people go online anymore so find a friend) and to realize how difficult it is to manage your own lil island then go buy this, hell it's Steam anyway. Price too high? Steam Sale!

Writing this has been harder then any review i've written on steam. Despite how much I love Tropico I was still on the fence wether i'd actually recommend this over 4.
