It's the sorta game that for everything it upgrades, it downgrades something else. First of all I don't remember the AI being this stupid in Tropico 4. Since you can't control your army directly this is pretty damning. I once lost because my army refused to stand and fight despite being much stronger. I had general 5 on my presidente, I had army drills, and even gave tropicans the right to own guns which all buff my army. But my army wouldn't fight. They would instead run away from the invading troops as they took potshots at my troops.

Yes, the troops would literally run away from the enemy because they felt they had to fight at the location the enemy was going instead of standing and fighting. This was not a one time thing either, this has happened multiple times with my army losing because of this, or because one of my squads would run past a battle in progress to go to another place.

Beyond this it feels like you have a lot less freedom to build your city then you did in 4. At first I thought the game was a lot harder then 4 but this quickly changed. I realized that the game isn't hard, it's just very linear. You build your city the way tropico intended for you to. You build entertainment and clinics next to your houses instead of having set 'districts' like an actual town would because if a building is too far away your people will refuse to drive there. Infact how close a building needed to be for the people to actually use it was a thing that continued to haunt me.

But I eventually hit my stride in that I realized the exact constitution options the game wanted me to take, and the 'correct' things to built in order to have a strong economy. For example in the colonial era you build cocoa, wool, and cotton and you're fine. In the world wars era you build textile mills to turn the wool and cotton into cloth, and boom. You're rich. I tried multiple other strategies but I continued to be money starved. Selling food is never that viable, lumber mills never sell enough to warrant the amount of island you'll not be able to build on because you'll need to allow trees to grow around it, and metal is a very finite thing all the way up until the cold wars era.

So why is this a recommendation? As stated earlier for everything removed or simplified is something added. The era system that I mentioned is very awesome and adds to the feeling of being El Presidente. No longer do you have only the russians and americans but instead you start out as a british colony, you become independant, you participate in the world wars, you endure the cold wars, and you finally go into modern times. No longer is it USSR and USA all the way through and this adds something to really getting into the game.

It's the sorta game that has the Civilization quality of "I'll just play up until I do this and then take a break." and then that turns into hours an suddenly the day is gone. Despite the problems I really, really like Tropico 5 and I have hopes that 6 will fix a lot of these issues.

I've always enjoyed the winking sense of humor in these games and Tropico 5 maintains the series' tradition with a goofy story for the main campaign that I was not expecting.  Gameplay is largely the same as previous entries - not a bad thing - with some added new buildings, edicts, and trade options.  One of the most notable additions is the family dynasty system and while I appreciated the added bonuses, they mostly come across as glorified managers.

On the negative side, there is a blandness to customizing your Island and I noticed this the most in regards to tourism and entertainment.  I would have preferred a better variety of tourist attractions, and while there are several options for gardens, after a few rounds every Island ends up looking exactly the same.

I also felt that the overlay system was woefully underdeveloped.  For a game that has many building providing services to local populations, the absence of a population denisty overlay seems like a big omission.  Having to use a separate menu to get to the overlays was also a big problem since selecting buildings would automatically select the overlay and take away your ability to cross-reference for planning (i.e. compare pollution to beauty).

I enjoyed this new Tropico enough to finish the main campaign but after that, I wasn't really interested in downloading any of the DLC or playing in sandbox mode.

In short, this is an enjoyable game. However, if you're considering getting it because you really liked Tropico 4, I would say stick with Tropico 4. There are a couple of ways that T5 improves upon T4, which I will list below, but for the most part T5 has fewer options and is less interactive - in short, far oversimplified. T4 is an overall better game.

Pros:
-Research that opens up possibilities during a specific age, as opposed to everything of that age automatically becoming available.
-City planning made easier with a well-conceived grid that takes the guesswork out of building and road placement.
-Military made more useful/necessary by increased rebel attack-rate when citizens unhappy (could be seen as a con, but it's just more incentive to try and treat your people well!)

Cons:
-Fewer building options.
-Can't have multiple types of the same building with different specializations.
-Adjusting wages is a hassle that should have a fix-all option (it does, but in my experience it does nothing).
-Elections just happen, there's no chance to make a speech or anything.
-Interactivity lessened by only featuring dialogue/quest options from major political figures, no longer interacting with movement figureheads, like the environmentalists or nationalists and so forth.

There are other cons, but once again, they're all relative to Tropico 4, so if you haven't played Tropico 4 you'll think nothing of it. But I would just say that the pros of Tropico 5 can easily be sacrificed for the far superior Tropico 4.

Is it different? Absolutely. Yet, as a long time fan of the series, I can honestly suggest this game. (I got it on sale for $10, and I suggest you get in on sale as well). I really just enjoy the content of this series, and this game is a decent enough continuation of the series.

The following concerns the game at medium difficulty settings.

[u]The campaign[/u]
The campaign includes only 4 different islands. You start with two that you can (or need to) switch after each mission. Constructed buildings will persist between missions on each island. Thus you only really need to build a good economy once and you are done for all remaining missions. The campaign is also rather short.

[u]Game mechanics[/u]
- [b]General buildings[/b]: Several buildings grant additional advantages if they are build on higher terrain. However, 3 of the 4 campaign islands are completely flat.

- [b]Housing[/b]: Compared to the previous Tropicos, the housing system has been improved. Even small buildings make sense now.

- Industry: Tropico 5 allows you to build larger industry production lines. You can start with a logging camp, then add a saw mill to generate planks and then use these planks to build furniture. That's quite a nice feature.

- Population: You can change a policy (~ every 5 years) that controls the number if immigrants. However, I never noticed any big difference between the options regarding the number of people arriving on my island. With open borders I got about 20 immigrants per ship. This leads to a problem, because you really need a lot of people on the island. The only other option is to increase the number of births by building clinics and hospital (up to 50% increase in births). But that's still not enough and I constantly ran out of workers (~200 workers missing in a population of 1400 people). This wouldn't be so bad if you didn't need to build lots of healthcare, religous and entertainment buildings to keep your population happy.

- [b]Unrest[/b]: The unrest system appears to be out of control. For example, even if the military faction loves you, they just might start a coup to get rid of you. Also, I haven't found any reliable way to get rid of rebels (However, they only became annoying in 2-3 missions, thus it might be due to scripting).

- [b]Military[/b]: The military mechanics are just horrible. Certain buildings are marked as targets once rebells or other forces attack. All your armys will then start moving towards these targets, ignoring any enemy forces that they may encounter on their way. The enemy will shoot at you though! This often leads to several causalties before your army even starts fighting back.
There is also an option to build an aircraft carrier that does not work at all, because the aircrafts won't fire if the enemy is close to buildings, which is usually the case. However, you can set it on "fire at will", which will make them shoot and set your buildings on fire. That would be perfectly okay, if the rockets would actually damage enemies that are moving, but it appears that they mostly do damage on stationary enemies.
Tropico 4 gave you more control over the movement of your armies, which made it much better in this respect.

- [b]Dealing with criminals, rebels, etc.[/b]: Similar to the previous tropico you can banish, arrest or kill people that you don't like. Or... well, you can at least issue the order to arrest them. Apparently the police doesn't really care about it. It takes years for them to take them to the prison.

All in all it's an okay game, but I wouldn't buy it again. Get Tropico 4 instead of Tropico 5.

I wanted to like this game. I spent a great deal of time searching for a game just like this one, read reviews, and finally decided that it was the one I wanted. Dropped $50 for the whole collection, and I will likely not play it again after the 150 or so hours I dropped into it.

Good

It is world-building, political gameplay that I was searching for in a sense. Much of the game allows you to control all of the little details that make the world your creating exactly what you want--for a while. The various constitution options were interesting, and it was one of the options that I found to be the most exciting, being able to control the type of people who come onto your island, controlling the state of the government, and setting up the professionalism of your military are all excellent options that I think really contribute to the overall feel of the game.

Bad

Execution of the above failed. The politics are largely one-way. You pick a side and can't really play the middle in any meaningful way if you want to complete a mission. In major-global conflicts, there is a political out if you are skilled enough. Not an option.

The game provides a limited and hilariously unsatisfactory tutorial that fails to explain most of the important aspects of the game that determine approval rating, military tactics, and government effects of a number of aspects. Moreover, most of the constitution is written to be funny rather than informative (along with quests, objectives, and so on), meaning that it is impossible to tell the exact effect most actions or changes will have until it is too late. And I say too late, because you can only alter the constitution once every five years. At one point, I altered mine and my approval rating dropped nearly 30% rapidly.

In regard to approval, it is almost a meaningless measure. Having an approval rating of 90+ is pretty safe, but as soon as you drop to 80 or so (keep in mind that U.S. Presidents largely have approval ratings of ~50%), rebellions happen constantly unless you are eliminating rebels (which is expensive). The further it falls, the more impossible it becomes to return the approval to the higher rating, largely because the constant threats result in rebellions, resulting in destroyed property, resulting in lacking the funds to rebuild the buildings that increase approval or eliminate the rebels that destroy them.

The military aspect of the game is useless. You can build a powerful military, but it ignores half of the threats that you come into contact with throughout the game. I lost several games because I had military units who refused to defend the palace. In other cases, the military units associate the battle with a specific location, that may not actually be associated with the battle, resulting in buildings (like guard towers) which get destroyed because your military is off defending a building and refuse to march to the actual location of the fight.

All and all, the game was goo for a couple of yucks, but ultimately is so frustrating to play, do to a lack of sufficient information from the game designer and buggy units that I cannot recommend it.

Tropico 5 is not the best Tropico game. It may be the first Tropico game available for Macs on Steam but it doesn't even include the full game - there is no Mission/Map Editor in the Mac version. Every game after Tropico 2 has been nearly identical. Each game adding one new thing each along with updated graphics and a decline in the players ability to micromanage and follow whats happening on your island.

Specifically about Tropico 5, though, is the issue with replayability. The Map Generator doesn't add as much variance to sandbox games as it once did. Your starting scenario is really only effected by how hard you make island Politics and Economy. You can't start the game with a strategy or gimmick in mind because a Very Wet climate island is only half covered in trees, Abundant Resources will only guarantee 3 fish deposits, and you can reliably find at least one spot on every single island for each crop. These are examples.

The trade mechanic is neat but it's paper thin and doesn't functionally add very much new to the gameplay. The Era's idea is neat. I like the concept of it but each era transition results in an invasion and 95% of your game strategy is forced to change on each transition. It functionally railroads you, specially when the first 1-2 hours of every map is on a time limit due to the first era being a "Colonial Mandate" that is always running out. Not to mention the fact that you can't just invent your islands backstory - it bakes post-colonial politics into every single island with cars.

I play Tropico games for the first 8 hours of every map. I dream up some neat/interesting/challenging/weird gimmick or handicap or economic/political focus and see if I can pull it off. The strength of Tropico 1, 2, and 3 was your ability to dictate the parameters of your game from the start and play a new and different game every time. Tropico 5 is just the one game that you can choose to look greener or browner, bigger or smaller, more rocky or less rocky.

The only reason I still play it is because earlier Tropicos aren't available on Mac on steam.

If you loved Tropico 4, Don't buy this game.

Short version: If you liked previous Tropico games, definitely get this one. If you haven't played the series, it'd still be an excellent introduction to this tongue-in-cheek city builder.

I started at 3, and 4 was just 3 but with new maps and an engine upgrade. But 5 is a proper sequel, with improved QoL and an overhaul of many mechanics. Primarily, the game is now separated into four "Eras" akin to the ages in Age of Empires: Colonial, World Wars, Cold War (ie, when Tropico 3 takes place), and Modern Times (when Tropico 4 takes place). Each era gates what buildings, edicts, and improvements are available, as well as what research can be done, because Research is now a mechanic in Tropico 5.

5 also introduces the Constitution as a mechanic, which effectively is your "build" for the island, even though you can change it through amendments after enough time has passed. Previous mechanics like your immigration policy have been folded into it, but it also includes other things like determining who can vote and how much you are willing to give up certain powers to improve the island's Liberty score. Essentially, you can now lean more heavily into being an iron-fisted dictator, a free democracy, or somewhere in between, and get bonuses that help you do it. Just be aware that the less free options come with caveats. (Nothing a sufficiently large and loyal military won't solve, though)

Speaking of the military, 5 makes it a much more important aspect of the game. In 3/4 you could probably get by with ignoring the military buildings by just keeping the population sufficiently happy. You can't do that in 5, and this is a good thing. Besides rebels, you also have to deal with things like pirates or sufficiently annoyed foreign powers; invasions are no longer an instant-lose condition but instead result in an enemy force invading your island that you have to fight off. Plus, more campaign objectives require you to have a large enough army to defend yourself. This can happen as early as the colonial era if you choose to fight for independence instead of buying it.

The campaign is excellent. Instead of every level being stand-alone, you now swap between two islands that progress through the eras, and more importantly, preserve whatever state you left them in before. Also, you now have a "Dynasty" of Presidente and their family members; whoever isn't the currently elected head of Tropico can be assigned to a building. Your Swiss account is no longer just a mechanic for scoring, but can be used for some mission objectives, as well as for improving your Dynasty members, improving the bonuses they give.

While there is an excess of DLC of questionable quality, the base game is fantastic, and the two biggest DLCs - Waterborne and Espionage - each come with well-made mini-campaigns that easily justify their prices.

Definitely a recommendation for Tropico vets and new players.

I've played all of the Tropico games since the beginning, but this is the one I go back to again and again. The balance and re-playability of this one just seem to be superior to all the others, even the newest one. I find myself getting so wrapped up building the perfect island that hours pass by without my realizing it, very easy to get lost in this one. The customization options, the Missions, the Workshop Missions, the sandbox, the ability to create your own customized missions, makes for endless variations. My single, solitary complaint (and it's a small one) is that once your island reaches a certain size - around 3,500 residents - regardless of how happy they are, people just start to leave and stop immigrating. You can have 99 scores on every metric - religion, jobs, housing, healthcare, etc. - no unemployed, no homeless, etc. - and mess with your Edicts and Constitution endlessly, but it's like once the island reaches a certain level of perfection, almost a Utopia-like society, people just leave for no reason. You find your businesses missing workers and can't hire anymore unless you pay foreigners to come, your residential buildings emptying, etc. 
Anyway - aside from that, it's a heck of a lot of fun to play Tropico 5, highly recommend.
